title: Developer Experience Docs: SDK Guides, Quickstarts, API Examples, and Top Support Issues (Playbook)
author: Ava Thompson
abstract: A single-source playbook for Developer Experience (DevEx) documentation covering SDK guides, quickstarts and templates, canonical API examples, docs-site operating procedures, and the top support issues with canonical fixes.
body:
## Purpose
This playbook defines standards and operational procedures for Developer Experience documentation at Redwood Inference. It is intended for docs owners, maintainers, SDK authors, and on-call engineers who triage developer-reported issues. The goal is to keep our docs accurate, discoverable, and actionable so engineering teams can ship against the Redwood API with minimal friction.

## Scope
- SDK reference guides (Python, JavaScript, Go, Java)
- Quickstarts and templates for common integration patterns
- Canonical API examples (curl, HTTP, SDKs)
- Docs-site operating procedures (publishing, rollback, audit)
- Known top support issues and canonical fixes

## Ownership and Roles
- Docs owner: Ava Thompson (eng-developer-experience) \u2014 overall ownership of the DevEx playbook and templates.
- SDK owners: individual SDK leads (see related_pages for per-SDK owner list).
- Reviewer pool: Maya Patel, Ethan Rodriguez, Liam Chen (technical review for accuracy).
- On-call: Platform on-call rotates weekly; docs bugs that cause customer-facing regressions route to oncall@redwood.com.

## Docs Site Operating Procedures
1. Release cadence
   - Minor edits (typos, small clarifications): continuous deploy to staging; auto-publish to production every 24 hours.
   - Major changes (API surface, security, behavior): gated release with at least two technical reviewers + product sign-off; publish window 09:00\u201317:00 PT to minimize global impact.
2. Review checklist (required before publish)
   - [ ] API surface changes reviewed by SDK owner.
   - [ ] Code samples compile and run locally (unit smoke test).
   - [ ] Quickstarts include expected output examples.
   - [ ] Related pages and links validated.
   - [ ] Labels/tags set for discoverability.
3. Rollback procedure
   - If a published change causes broken examples or customer regressions:
     a) Create an incident ticket and notify #devex in Slack.
     b) Revert to previous content version via docs-site admin panel.
     c) Run smoke tests for the reverted page(s).
     d) Post a short incident note on the page change log and notify impacted teams.
4. Audit and QA
   - Quarterly doc audits per SDK: check for API drift, deprecated endpoints, and changed defaults.
   - Maintain a test harness that runs sample snippets daily against staging to catch runtime regressions.

## SDK Guide Structure (standard template)
- Title and one-line summary
- Quickstart (60\u2013120s) with runnable example
- Full reference (methods, args, return types)
- Error handling & troubleshooting section
- Migration notes (for breaking changes)
- FAQ & common gotchas
- Changelog and release notes link

Example quickstart header for Python:

"""
# Quickstart: Python SDK (text generation)
from redwood import RedwoodClient
client = RedwoodClient(api_key=\"$REDWOOD_API_KEY\")
response = client.generate(prompt=\"Write a short product summary for Redwood Inference.\")
print(response.text)
"""

Minimum checks for SDK quickstarts:
- Use latest stable SDK version in examples.
- Include environment variable usage for credentials.
- Keep responses deterministic where possible (set seed or max_tokens).

## Quickstarts and Templates (catalog)
- Text generation quickstarts: Python, JS, Go
- Chat integrations: Node.js express middleware template
- Embeddings + vector search: Python + FAISS starter template
- Reranking pipeline: Python example with top-k retrieval
- Webhook/streaming example: Node.js streaming client

Each template must include:
- README with integration steps
- Dockerfile (if containerized)
- Minimal config.yaml with required fields (API host, API key, model)

Config.yaml example (as plain text):

api_host: https://api.redwood.ai
api_key_env: REDWOOD_API_KEY
model: redwood/text-bison-v1
max_tokens: 256

## Canonical API Examples
Provide short, copy-paste examples for common developer flows. Keep examples small and focused.

Curl example \u2014 text generation:

curl -s -X POST "https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate" \\
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_API_KEY" \\
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \\
  -d '{"model":"redwood/text-bison-v1","input":"Summarize the benefits of Redwood Inference in one paragraph."}'

Python SDK example (sync):

from redwood import RedwoodClient
client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY'))
resp = client.generate(model=\"redwood/text-bison-v1\", input=\"Translate the following to French: Hello world.\")
print(resp.text)

JS example (streaming):

import Redwood from '@redwood/inference-sdk'
const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY })
const stream = client.streamGenerate({ model: 'redwood/chat-compact-v1', input: 'Write a commit message for: fix typo in README' })
for await (const chunk of stream) { process.stdout.write(chunk) }

## Top Support Issues and Canonical Fixes (current top 10)
1) "401 Unauthorized" in examples
   - Symptoms: curl/SDK calls return 401 immediately.
   - Root cause: missing or expired API key; environment variable not set in container.
   - Canonical fix: Ensure REDWOOD_API_KEY is set in runtime; for containers, set via secrets manager and document in template. Add troubleshooting note: run `echo $REDWOOD_API_KEY` (locally) or `kubectl get secret` (k8s).
2) Broken code samples after SDK release
   - Symptoms: examples fail with TypeError or missing method.
   - Root cause: SDK public surface changed without updating docs.
   - Canonical fix: coordinate SDK release with docs change. Use pre-release CI job that runs example smoke tests against SDK rc. Revert doc commit and notify SDK owner if regression detected.
3) Streaming responses hang or never finish
   - Symptoms: example client never receives end-of-stream.
   - Root cause: incorrect handling of chunked transfer encoding or missing event finalizer in examples.
   - Canonical fix: include minimal streaming client that listens for the stream-complete event; sample code for Node.js and Python.
4) Embedding dimension mismatch with vector store
   - Symptoms: runtime errors inserting vectors into FAISS/Annoy.
   - Root cause: model variant changed embedding dimensionality.
   - Canonical fix: document expected embedding size in quickstart and include a runtime assertion in sample code: `assert len(embedding) == 1536`.
5) Example latency much higher than docs claim
   - Symptoms: quickstart reports 500\u2013800ms, production sees 1.5\u20132s.
   - Root cause: using non-batched / debug endpoints, or sample model mismatch (cheap vs production).
   - Canonical fix: update quickstart to use production model names, note batching recommendations, and include a note on expected p50/p95 under default settings.
6) Incorrect error handling: uncaught exceptions in samples
   - Symptoms: sample app crashes on network blips.
   - Root cause: missing retry/backoff logic and lack of graceful degradation.
   - Canonical fix: add a simple retry decorator and fallback to cached responses; include recommended backoff (exponential, max 3 attempts).
7) Mismatched content-type or JSON encoding
   - Symptoms: API returns 400 with parsing error.
   - Root cause: example uses single quotes or incorrectly encoded payload.
   - Canonical fix: standardize on JSON.dumps in Python examples and include correct curl quoting patterns.
8) Function calling / tool calling examples out-of-date
   - Symptoms: generated output doesn't include function calls as described.
   - Root cause: model capabilities or API parameters changed.
   - Canonical fix: maintain a short integration test that validates function-calling behavior across published model variants; update examples and note model compatibility.
9) Private deployment quickstarts missing networking notes
   - Symptoms: private customers cannot connect to control plane or runtime.
   - Root cause: omitted instructions for firewall and VPC peering rules.
   - Canonical fix: add a networking checklist (egress to telemetry endpoints, API host IP ranges, DNS entries) to the private deployment quickstarts.
10) Confusing example defaults for content filtering and safety
   - Symptoms: examples show permissive safety settings and produce content that fails compliance tests.
   - Root cause: sample config uses permissive flags for brevity.
   - Canonical fix: add a safety section to quickstarts explaining defaults and include a secure-by-default config block.

## Troubleshooting Playbook (short)
- Step 1: Reproduce the issue locally using the exact example in the docs.
- Step 2: Check SDK version and API host: `pip show redwood-inference` / `npm ls @redwood/inference-sdk` / `go list -m all`.
- Step 3: Run smoke tests in docs CI and capture logs.
- Step 4: If broken sample, revert docs and file a coordinated fix with SDK owner.

## Metrics and KPIs for Docs Health
- Number of doc-based support tickets opened per month (target < 50).
- Example success rate in CI smoke tests (target 100%).
- Time to triage docs regressions (target < 4 hours business).
- Search click-through rate for quickstarts (monitor weekly).

## Appendix: Useful snippets and templates
- Standard headers for quickstarts (copyable): title, one-liner, environment, run steps, expected output.
- Standard Dockerfile snippet: `FROM python:3.11-slim; COPY . /app; RUN pip install -r requirements.txt; CMD ["python", "main.py"]`.
- Contact points: docs@redwood.ai (general), sdk-owners@redwood.ai (API/SDK regressions), oncall@redwood.com (urgent).
